subtopic: SIGNING OF THE NATO-EUROPEAN DEFENCE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Could the minister make a statement on the signing of the agreements concerning Germany yesterday and today, and how it affects Canada-if Canada is affected. I regret that I have given the minister only short notice.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SIGNING OF THE NATO-EUROPEAN DEFENCE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be glad to make a short statement on this important question of the signature of certain documents in Bonn yesterday and in Paris today, and their effect upon this country.
Today in Paris members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization signed a protocol to extend the guarantees under article 5 of the treaty to the European defence community. The protocol was signed on behalf of Canada by Mr. A. D. P. Heeney, the permanent representative of Canada on the North Atlantic council.
Hon. members will recall that on March 21, when reporting on the Lisbon meeting of the North Atlantic council, I mentioned the approval in principle by the council of this extension of security guarantees, which means in fact that, if the international undertakings are all ratified, our guarantees will cover the territory of the Federal Republic of Germany and the forces of the Federal Republic serving in the European army when in the area covered by the North Atlantic treaty. The European defence community, for its part, gives a reciprocal guarantee to NATO. In other words, the European army, of which German forces will form a part, will be available for NATO defence in western Europe and, in fact, will come under NATO command.
The exchange of guarantees will be brought about by the ratification of a series of agreements. If hon. members will permit, I should like to mention the various related agreements, for although Canada is a party to only one of them, all these undertakings bear on the final result.
The first group of documents are commonly known as the contractual arrangements, and consist of agreements between the three occupying powers-France, the United Kingdom and the United States of America, on the one hand, and the Federal Republic of Germany, on the other. They are designed to replace the occupation statute because Russian tactics in the four power conferences have prevented agreement on a formal German peace treaty. The effect of these peace contracts, which were signed in Bonn yesterday, will be to restore West Germany's autonomy except in certain limited spheres which are reserved to the former occupying powers.
Today the second series of documents, the European defence treaty and its related protocols, have been signed in Paris by representatives of France, Italy, Belgium, Luxembourg, The Netherlands, and the Federal Republic of Germany. The main purpose of this treaty is to establish the European army, to which each of the signatory powers will contribute forces. Canada is not, Mr. Speaker, a party to the European defence treaty and our forces in Europe will not form part of the European army. One of the protocols to the European defence treaty, however, extends the security guarantees of the treaty to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, of which we are a member.
Also today in Paris, as I have just indicated, NATO members have signed the NATO protocol to reciprocate this guarantee. This is the only document in this rather complex series of international undertakings to which Canada is formally a party. If hon. members are agreeable, I would suggest that the text of this protocol, which is quite short but which is very important, be printed as an appendix to Hansard. These international undertakings are, as I have said already, subject to ratification and in due course, before ratification by Canada, indeed I hope during the present session, parliament will be given the opportunity for a full discussion of this NATO-European defence community protocol.
Hon. members may wish when we are discussing the NATO protocol to discuss the other related documents which I have mentioned. Of course, they will not be before the house for approval. Nevertheless, as they have an important bearing on our commitments under the NATO protocol, I shall

Excise Tax Act
arrange for copies to be available to hon. members as soon as they can be obtained for distribution.

speechtext: The officials of the Department of National Revenue will be here in a moment, but so far as I am aware no difficulty has been encountered in administering the act with respect to those particular drugs. Possibly the Minister of National Revenue has some other information. He confirms what I have just said.

I think the information which the minister has given to the committee will help to dissipate the fears which some hon. members seemed to have or which apparently were entertained by the government in connection with exempting drugs of this kind. Without proposing to launch into a debate on the subject may I express the hope that in the light of the past year's experience with these four drugs the government will give serious and early consideration to an extension of this list to include other similar drugs.
There are many people who are under a heavy burden of expense as a result of being required under medical advice to take certain forms of drugs constantly. Some of these drugs are exceedingly expensive and in the case of chronic sufferers who are under heavy
[Mr. Pearson.)
expense it seems to me that there is a clear case for an extension of the exemptions in the field of drugs.

I should like to place on the record a short memorandum dealing with the operation of the Excise Tax Act. I am not doing this in the hope that anything can be done at the moment but simply to have it on the record for consideration. It points out an anomaly which exists according to the way in which merchandising is done.
Under the existing sales and excise tax regulations, the base upon which taxes apply is the price at which the merchandise is sold by the manufacturer. This is known as the ad valorem method of tax calculation.
Under this method a tire manufacturer who sells a special brand tire to a tire merchandiser accounts for his tax on the basis of his selling price which probably takes the form of a cost plus a profit factor. The special marketer then does not pay these taxes on his selling and administrative expenses or on his profit.
The manufacturer that markets his own name brand tire must account for his tax on the higher price at which he sells his merchandise to his dealer trade and thus must pay the tax on both his selling and administrative expense and his profit.
Just what this differential might be in terms of cost plus tax would work out differently but it is our opinion that the special brand marketer is handed about a 5 per cent cost advantage over the standard brand marketer simply as a result of the method of application of tax to the basic buying price.
Thus by the means of use of tax application, the manufacturer finds it actually cheaper to market his products through a marketer who uses other than his own name brand and this seems most inequitable.
As I say, I place this on the record, not in the hope that it will be dealt with today but that it will be considered by the department in due course.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 205, to amend the Income Tax Act.

Before this bill is read the second time I want to make a few comments. This bill of course introduces amendments to the Income Tax Act in order to give effect to some of the budget resolutions. I think it would be well for us to consider for a few moments the terms of this legislation, in the light of Liberal party policy. During recent weeks we have heard a great deal of the way in which the government ignored the wishes of the House of Commons-I shall have more to say about that later. We have heard very few Liberal speakers during the past few weeks having much to say on the announced official policy of the Liberal party, possibly because of the extent to which fiscal policy is ignored in the amendment that is now before the house.
I have before me a copy of a resolution that was adopted by the national Liberal convention in 1948. I think it was No. 14 on the agenda. It is headed, "Sound fiscal policy." The resolution in part has this to say:
The tax burden should as far as possible be distributed equitably and in accordance with ability to pay. In reducing taxes first consideration should be given to easing the burden of the lowest income groups.
I want to contrast with that resolution the minister's consideration as expressed to this house on former occasions, and as exemplified in the amendments before us.
According to official Liberal policy, in reducing taxes first consideration should be given to easing the burden of the lowest income groups. When the minister was introducing his budget resolutions, as a matter of fact when he was introducing his budget, his first

consideration was not that of the lowest income groups, certainly his first expressed consideration was not for that group. The one group for which the minister expressed deep concern, as reported in Hansard at page 1252, was given in these words:
Quite frankly, I am concerned that conditions make it necessary to maintain in our tax structure rates as high as this on business profits.
If you read that budget speech you will fail to find anywhere in it any consideration for the income tax payer in the lowest income group, such as is expressed in these words for the tax on business profits.
In keeping with the minister's consideration, as expressed in his budget speech, he does provide some small measure of relief for a certain group of corporations. As a matter of fact, one tax reduction-if it can be called a tax reduction at all-that was proposed by the minister was not proposed for those in the lowest income groups, but was for a certain group of corporations. The measures proposed by the minister would place a ceiling of 43 per cent on the tax paid by that special group of corporations under the Income Tax Act.
I said earlier, and I repeat, that neither I nor any of us in this group feel the same concern for the corporations' need of tax relief as does the minister or as in fact do the members of the official opposition.
The statistics presented by the dominion bureau of statistics in a booklet entitled "National Income" show us that in 1951 corporation profits before taxes were paid were $2,850 million, the highest in Canada's history. These gross profits were $400 million greater in 1951 than in 1950, a percentage increase over 1950 of 16 per cent. The dividends paid to Canadians in 1951 amounted to a flat $300 million, again the highest dividends paid to Canadians in any year in our history.
The undistributed profits of all these business concerns are included in the dominion bureau of statistics figures. The undistributed profits in 1951 amounted to $710 million, and were exceeded by only two other years in our history, namely 1948 and 1950. The profits retained in Canada after payment of taxes and after the distribution of dividends outside of Canada amounted to $1,037 million, again the highest profits retained in Canada by Canadian business in the history of our country, the highest on record.
It is in the light of these statistics that we feel the minister's concern was slightly misplaced; that instead of being concerned for those who, according to the national Liberal convention, should have his concern, he was much more concerned for the interests of the corporations and their taxation.
Income Tax Act
Corporation taxes collected by the minister in 1951 exceeded his own estimates by about 12 per cent; and the minister himself admitted during his budget speech that much of his surplus, which has been so much criticized across the country, resulted from the excess of corporation taxes over the minister's own estimates.
If you compare the position of corporations in regard to taxes in Canada with that other great capitalist country to the south, the United States, you will find that Canadian business and Canadian corporations come off fairly easily. In the United States corporations pay a regular federal tax of 52 per cent, apart from their state corporation tax, plus an excess profits tax of 30 per cent. It is estimated that the average United States corporation pays a 60 per cent corporation tax, as compared with Canada's top federal corporation tax of 43 to 45 per cent, or a top of 52 to 54 per cent when provincial corporation tax and old age security tax are added.
It is in the light of those facts, Mr. Speaker, that I am of the opinion that the minister not only ignores the wishes of parliament, but feels sufficiently secure to completely ignore the resolutions by the national convention of his own party. There is no such concern expressed in the minister's speeches for those in the lower income groups as I have pointed out was expressed on behalf of the corporations. There was a phony decrease announced. At page 1254 of Hansard for April 8, 1952, the minister said:
. . . the average taxpayer will pay 6 per cent less than he would otherwise have done under the income tax law as it now stands.
That is at the time the minister was speaking. The minister did not feel that it was necessary to mention the fact that the Income Tax Act as it then stood had not been in effect for a full year, nor did he point out that the so-called 6 per cent reduction in the average income tax actually meant an increase in the 1952 tax over that actually paid in 1951. The minister's concern for corporations took the form of some slight relief granted, but his concern for the lower income groups, to whom his party's annual convention called attention, took the form of an increase in the 1952 taxes over those imposed in 1951, and that without taking the special social security tax into consideration.
As proof of that, of course, it has been pointed out that a single person with an income of $2,000 paid $165 in taxes in 1951, while in 1952 the same person with the same income will pay $175. A married

Income Tax Act
man with an income of $3,000 and without any children is in exactly the same position. Whereas his 1951 tax was $165, his 1952 tax will be $175. As though the minister wanted to add insult to injury so far as those in the lower income tax groups were concerned, he has not been content with raising the income tax for those groups but he increases the tax in the lower brackets at a higher rate than he does in the upper brackets. For example, a married man without children earning $3,000 of income finds his 1952 tax increased over his 1951 tax by 12 per cent. A married man without children in the $20,000 income bracket finds his 1952 tax increased only 6 per cent over his 1951 tax.
Before this bill is adopted, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is worth calling attention to these facts, and the extent to which the minister can ignore the so-called sound fiscal policy of the national Liberal convention. I submit that the minister's disregard of the policy expressed by that same convention may be seen in the 2-2-2 formula for financing old age security. We are told that 42 per cent of the funds necessary to finance old age security will come from the sales tax, a tax which is particularly burdensome to those in the lower income groups. It would seem to me that if the minister had the same concern for those in the lower income groups that he showed for the corporations, he would at least have made some concession, either in a reduction in the sales tax or in some other adjustment in his 2-2-2 formula. We are to Id that 16-1 per cent of the necessary funds to finance this old age security will come from the personal income tax, only 14-9 per cent from the corporation tax and 27 per cent from the general revenue fund.
The removal of the $60 maximum payment, and a graduated income tax for the support of the old age security program, would have been much more in line with the policy enunciated by the national Liberal convention than is the policy which the minister is following today. There is no reduction in the sales tax, but a slight reduction in corporation taxes. Apparently the wishes of the national Liberal convention can be disregarded by the minister with the same abandon as are the wishes of the House of Commons. I need only refer in passing to the minister's disregard of the express wish of the House of Commons in the matter of the 4 per cent floor on deductions for medical services.
At this point I might say to the minister that in my opinion the government made a mistake in rejecting the express wish of parliament in that matter. While the minister may argue that it was not a directive, that parliament merely suggested the minister

should give consideration, nevertheless there is no question in the world but that was the express wish of parliament and that it represented what parliament wanted done. The minister ignored them. Many of us who have followed the debates and the discussions during the recent by-elections must have been impressed by the fact that there was no single more telling argument against the Liberal government and the Liberal policy than the minister's rejection of the wishes of parliament in the matter of the removal of that 4 per cent.
It was unfortunate, of course, that the C.C.F., who introduced that measure, received little benefit from it during the by-elections. It would be just asking too much of ordinary human beings, of course, to give credit to political opponents during the heat of an election campaign. But during that campaign I discovered that the official opposition, from their criticism of the government for ignoring the will of parliament in the matter of that 4 per cent, were able to gain more effect than from their criticism of any other measure.
Possibly the government is still capable of learning something from the course of events. While it is asking too much to expect the minister to make any changes in the amending bill which is now before us, it may well be that we shall find-and we shall certainly hope to do so-some relief for those in the lower income brackets when the next budget is presented, particularly if that should be a pre-election budget.

Mr. Speaker, I do not like to delay the progress of the house by dealing at length with the various legislative measures under consideration and therefore my remarks will be very brief.
I wish to say at the outset that I have always liked to comment on the subject of income tax, as a representative of the wage earner. You know that, from the time I have been elected to this house, I have always shown the greatest interest in the welfare of the wage earner and the problem of income tax.
Just lately, I happened to read the report of the 65th general annual convention of the Montreal chamber of commerce. One of the sections of the report, section 8, deals with matters of federal jurisdiction. Here is an extract from that section:
Revision of the Income Tax Act.
The chamber wishes the federal government to base the Income Tax Act upon the following princinles:
1. The taxpaver must benefit from an income tax exemption at least equal to the minimum amount required to insure his family's livelihood.

2. All taxpayers must be treated alike with respect to the income tax levied on the income above that minimum amount.
Everybody will agree that I have always advocated these two principles for the benefit of the taxpayers I have mentioned.
Owing to the fact that the cost of living index, which had already hit the 125-1 per cent mark, still had a tendency to rise even higher, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) as early as July 1946 to put the basic exemption back at the $1,200 level for single taxpayers and at $2,000 for married people.
I brought up the subject again the following year when expressing my views on the budget; the statement I made at that time is to be found on page 3344 of the English Hansard of May 22, 1947. I had then quoted figures to show that due to the exemption allowed at that time, much lower than the one in effect nowadays, the single person whose annual income was $1,200 had a deficit of $99 and that this deficit amounted to $215 when the taxpayer with an annual income of $2,000 was a married man with two children. At this time, the cost of living index was still rising; a jump of 8 per cent had brought it to 133-1 per cent.
And as before and for the same reasons I renewed my appeal to the government, in March, 1948, since the cost of living had by then reached 150-8 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, any member who belonged to the working class before he came to this house can much more readily understand that group's plight and that is why I made those comments in March 1949. On their behalf I asked the Minister of Finance to show greater consideration for that section of our population. I did ask for a higher basic exemption, namely $1,500 for the single taxpayer and $2,500 for the married man, and I dare say that those amounts would not have been excessive, considering the fact that the cost of living index had then reached the 159.2 per cent mark.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance looks upon the past year with great satisfaction. Our minister obviously is very busy and he cannot meet middle class people as often as he would like. On the other hand, he is in touch continually with his financial advisers and I am led to believe they know how to give him a rosy outlook on life.
I am the more convinced of the fact from having been made acquainted with the Income Tax Act and the exemptions it allows. There is no encouragement for wage-earners. With their family burdens and the 55704-165J
Income Tax Act
present taxation they can hardly contemplate with much satisfaction, in the light of this legislation, the past year and the year ahead.
The minister has stated once again that our difficulties stem from international affairs. We knew that and, as he pointed out, whether we like it or not, we must unfortunately bear with it for the sake of enduring peace.
Mr. Speaker, I have already indicated the deficit of these middle class people for 1947, when the cost of living index stood at 133 per cent. But at the end of 1951, the cost of living index had risen to 191 per cent. These people must also have been affected by the rise.

I dare hope our commitments will not be so heavy in the future and that at the next budget my remarks will be kept in mind with a view to allowing the wage earner of Canada a sufficient exemption to provide for the minimum of income required to sustain his family. This income, unfortunately, he has not today.

Mr. Speaker, I have been looking Bill No. 205 over carefully and have been unable to find an item which appeared in the Trade News of April, 1952. It is a short item and I will just put it on the record. It is headed: "Taxation Ruling" and reads as follows:
Canadian deep-sea fishermen, operating as coadventurers on a share of the catch have been authorized by the Department of National Revenue to average their earnings over a five-year period for income tax purposes, and also to deduct their away-from-home food and accommodation expenses. This applies to all deep-sea fishermen in Canada including captains, engineers and cooks, as well as those fishing on schooners, trawlers and draggers under the general form of agreement in common use in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island. This agreement provides for the sharing of catch returns. The individual fisherman will still be required to file his income tax return each year and at that time will pay the tax owing, but at the end of five years he can work out the average of his net earnings and obtain a refund if he is entitled to one.
The privilege to average earnings only applies if the following stipulations are made: the fishermen must file their returns for the previous year by April 30 for each following year, and in the last year of the five-year period they must file their election to average their returns for the previous five years by April 30 following the last taxation year.

When one considers that a gentleman like Austin Taylor on the Pacific coast can run all over the country with his hay burners, and the fact that he is being given the privilege extended by this bill, one wonders at once why fishermen of the description I have given are not considered at the same time.
This is a serious matter. As I said at the outset, consideration was given for some time to this problem; but under present-day conditions fishermen are being denied the privilege of averaging income or of deducting away-from-home living expenses. The men I have in mind operate usually two to a boat, and some of the boats are 50 to 100 feet long. They are big freighters, and usually carry a crew of two. These freighters are away from home nine-tenths of the time. Many of the crew were fishermen for years, and did nothing but fish. However, owing to their qualifications as navigators they have been chosen to operate in this particular branch of the industry. They work on a share basis; none of the men mentioned would be on wages or salary, but rather on a share of the profits.
I would ask the minister and his officials to give this matter serious consideration, because in the minds of those who have been denied the privilege there is the thought that discrimination is being shown. They are bona fide fishermen; their incomes fluctuate in exactly the same way and to the same extent as other men engaged in the industry. If the sardine catch is good, their incomes increase; if the sardine catch is low, their

incomes diminish. Over a five-year period their incomes would fluctuate to the same extent as those of the other fishermen I have mentioned.
Then, I have pointed out that their away-from-home expenses have been denied them. I was on the water a great many years myself, and I realize that away-from-home expenses are, as a rule, much greater than the expenses when one is at his own home. Perhaps only a very few of us are fancy cooks, the majority having to depend on food in a ready-to-eat state, which costs a great deal more than it would at home. I would ask the minister to give this matter his serious consideration, because these men should be given exactly the same treatment accorded the others in the industry.

Mr. Speaker, on the theory that the constant dripping of water will eventually wear away a stone I shall once again direct the minister's attention to a few observations I made to his parliamentary assistant. First of all, I must say that I was very interested in hearing the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin), a Liberal member, make a plea for the increasing of the exemptions to $3,000 for married persons. It is interesting to note the effect of by-elections on the succeeding day. I support the member in his plea and I am sure that many members on the opposite side of the house were also pleased to hear this first Liberal member make this plea. I fully expect to see him followed by a succession of hon. members before this debate is over.
I think there are sound grounds for bringing more equity into our income tax structure by doing what the great trade union bodies have asked the government to do and which great numbers of people in this country expect them to do, that is to raise the exemption for married people to $3,000 and for single persons to $2,000. I am not going to add much to what I said before, but I do think that when one realizes the cost of living and the circumstances that exist today with regard to housing, rent and all the things necessary to maintain the human body, it is a most reasonable request on the part of those who have made it. I have not the slightest hesitation in supporting it.
Once again I suggest to the minister that he give consideration to the expressed will of the house in the resolution that was adopted and which asked him to consider eliminating the four per cent floor under deductions for medical expenses. I think it was the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) who said that a great majority of the people think the government and the minister acted improperly or wrongly in not recognizing the expressed will of the house and giving effect to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Many of my constituents have written to me on this particular point-not only members

of my own party, but members of all parties

Before going on any further may I say that I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) make a plea for the granting of a deduction for the cost of maintaining a housekeeper in the case of illness and where a husband was left with dependent children. I know of a number of cases in my own constituency where the circumstances are tragic because of the burdens placed upon husbands. In several of the cases I know of, these men are working steadily at reasonably good wages but because they have to keep housekeepers and stand the additional expense of their maintenance they find the burden almost unbearable. I do think that consideration should be given to people in these circumstances. I know personally of three or four cases where men have used up their life savings in order to meet these costs and are now going into debt.
Once again I bring to the minister's attention a matter which I brought to the attention of his parliamentary assistant. I refer to the allowance of travelling costs incurred by workers at the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company who live anywhere from five to twenty miles away from their employment. These men have no other option but to live where they do. If they want to find a house to live in, if they want^ to have a place in which to bring up their families, they must live at varying distances from the plant.
When I broached the matter before, the parliamentary assistant's reply was that the government considered these expenses as being normal expenses. As I said before, I do not think you can deem expenses which run as high as $20 to $30 a month as being normal expenses. These workers must bear this cost as they are forced to travel from ten to forty miles per day back and forth from their employment. I suggest that the minister give consideration to exempting transportation costs incurred in going to and from employment when they are in excess of 25 or 30 cents per day. That would eliminate the ordinary street car or bus fares or cases where only short distances are travelled by motorcar and would at the same time be fair to people who must travel as much as ten to forty miles a day.
I have personal knowledge of the fact that these men travel mostly in buses owned by co-operative societies which have been formed
[Mr. Herridge.l
by themselves. These successful transportation co-operative societies have large capital investments in buses, cars and things of that sort. These societies worked all during the war and they are now providing transportation for these workers at cost. They are performing a good service to the community and the country by reducing expenses to their present point. I am quite sure that if these transportation services were being undertaken by private companies the expenses of the men would be almost doubled. Through co-operative action, through rank and file action by the men themselves, everything possible has been done to lower the cost of transportation. It has been reduced practically to cost and I do ask the minister to give consideration to my suggestion that transportation expenses to and from work above 25 or 30 cents a day be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes.
When the parliamentary assistant was dealing with the resolution I brought up the question of the allowance as a deduction of expenses incurred in forest conservation work. I had proceeded for some time and then I was told that I was out of order. It was suggested that I should bring the matter to the minister's attention on the second reading. I refer to companies and individuals who have rendered great service to Canada by spending money for the benefit of future generations.
They have carried on forest conservation work by planting trees, by thinning timber, by building trails and roads for fire protection. This policy has been advocated by the dominion government and by the provincial governments. It is getting increasing support throughout the country and more and more companies and individuals are carrying on this work at this time. I know of many small holders of timber limits in my own district who throughout the years, have spent a considerable amount in maintaining their forest holdings.
I think companies and individuals should receive some consideration for what I would term an acceptance of their social responsibility. They are spending money now from which they will receive no return in their lifetime; they are making an investment for future generations. I repeat that that sort of social responsibility should receive some consideration and I do urge the minister to consider allowing deductions up to a certain point for money invested by companies or individuals in the work of forest conservation and the maintenance of a great capital asset of this country, our forest resources.
The argument that I am presenting seems so logical from my point of view, possibly

because I have lived in the bush all my life, that I cannot understand its not receiving consideration. When the minister replies I would like him to tell me if under the present law and regulations arrangements have been made with any companies to permit deductions for the cost of carrying on forest conservation work in the way of building roads and trails, planting of trees and so on. I cannot understand why any government would fail to provide the necessary incentives to this worth-while work.

I should like to take this opportunity to ask the minister to reconsider the matter of assessment of farmers' incomes. I know he has considered it and I hope that he will consider it again. The average farmer operates as a unit. In my own case I raised four children, and while they were quite small they were doing work on the farm. If they had not done those jobs I would have had to pay wages to a man to do the work. I think some consideration should be given to that factor in the assessment of farmers' incomes. There are so many jobs that boys and girls of twelve years of age can do in the hay field. I have a grandson who can go out in the field and plow. It would cost $120 or $130 a month to hire a man to do the same work. There is no compensation for what he does. The minister need not take time to reply now because both he and the minister sitting behind him have told me before that if such a practice is started they do not know where it will end. I am concerned about justice for the farmer. I should like the minister to give the matter consideration and see if something cannot be done for the farmer who is working as a unit. He is taxed for all the income earned by five or six people, and he should only be taxed on his own income.

I think when I am finished the minister will see the reasonableness of my remarks, and it is because of the erosion that has taken place that I propose to make these remarks. Many people on the shores of the great lakes, whether they be farmers, fruit growers or other property owners, have been obliged to construct jetties, seawalls or embankments of one kind and another in order to protect their properties. Representations have been made to me by various property owners, and I am sure to other members on both sides of the house, that some consideration should be given to these people with respect to money expended to preserve their property in order that their revenues, for instance, may not be depreciated. I think it is only fair to bring this matter before the house because not only are fruit farmers and farmers generally affected but thousands of miles of lake and waterfront are involved.
The tourist industry is also affected so far as lake and riverfront property is concerned, and that is a matter of no small concern. My contention is that the minister should give consideration to the problem with which these people are faced. In order to preserve their property they have been obliged to build jetties, barricades or whatever may be recommended by engineers in order to prevent their property from being washed away into the waters of the various lakes or rivers. I know that applies to practically all the great lakes. To date the damage has amounted to millions. It is only recently that the property owners have realized that they themselves must do something and not be too dependent on the government. In any tax deductions that take place, consideration should be given to the amount of money that they have to spend, and consideration should also be given to the fact that they

will have to spend at least $500 or $1,000 this year and they may have to continue to do that for one or two years more.

All right; but our contention is that the philosophy behind this deductibility, as it was announced in those days, needs to be revised. But surely there is room for progress, and in my view the government should try to keep up with the thinking of the people in this country. There is growing more and more the feeling that it is common sense to try to deal with medical expenses on some co-operative or community basis.
The minister knows that I feel we should tackle that problem in a much more fundamental way, by a nation-wide program of health insurance, but we are having difficulty in persuading the government to move very fast in that direction. Meantime, here is one little step that could be taken to put medical

expenses to some extent on a community or social basis. After all, that is what it would do if the 4 per cent floor were removed. The result would be that those who have heavier medical expenses would get a larger income tax saving, and those with lesser expenses would get a smaller saving, whereas those with no medical expenses at all would not get a saving against income tax in that respect.
There is no doubt, too, that the idea of removing that floor has won very wide support. After all, the motion asking that the government consider removing that floor carried unanimously in this house on March 26.

The press welcomed the fact that in this instance a private member's motion had been passed by the house, and it particularly welcomed the fact that it was a motion dealing with this particular subject, namely, some relief to our people in respect of medical expenses.
In my view the case for it is unanswerable, and sooner or later the minister is going to have to make that change. I see no reason why he should not make it at this session, indeed right now while we are dealing with this bill. I dare to hope that the events of yesterday might suggest to the government that it was a mistake to oppose the wishes of parliament and of the people generally in respect of this matter. I would suggest that the government should give further thought to this question which is important on two counts. I suggested on a previous occasion, Mr. ^Speaker, that one of the places that revenue might be obtained to make up for whatever it might cost to wipe out the 4 per cent floor would be from corporations. I raised the question as to the disparity between there being a graduated tax on personal incomes and what to all intents and purposes is a flat tax on corporations. That was discussed with the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, who of course defended the present position. It is still my view, and it is a view that is expressed in the writings of a number of economists, that the graduated nature of a personal income tax is vitiated, particularly in the case of those in the higher brackets, when you have a flat tax on corporation income which is lower than the rates that apply to the upper brackets of personal income.
After all, what counts in terms of personal income, so far as the wealthy are concerned, is not only the actual dollars they take out of a corporation with which they may be

connected, but the increase in their economic power. I submit to the minister that there is room for increasing the corporation tax, and there is room for putting it on a graduated basis more comparable to that which applies to the personal income tax. In my view that would be fairer, and furthermore it would be a means of raising additional revenue.
In connection with this whole question, may I remind the minister that the Monetary Times, in its issue of May 1952, carries a comment on his budget which indicates that corporations generally feel that they are lucky to have the present minister in his portfolio. This comment is entitled "Individuals Pay More", and reads as follows:
Until the rearmament program is completed there are no grounds for expecting reductions in the corporation and personal income tax rates. With this year's spending program nearing the $4-5 billion mark businessmen have reason to be thankful the Minister of Finance is a staunch free enterprise man, who recognizes that excessive taxation on industry can kill the goose that lays the golden eggs. Though corporate taxes at 50 per cent are high-Abbott thinks it's about the limit-they are not so high as the combined corporate and excess profits taxes in the United States.
Abbott had to get more money this year and he has chosen the unpopular policy of taking it from individuals rather than loading more on business.
That, of course, is a comment from business , which regards taxation of business as something to be avoided, and the comment is that businessmen should feel lucky to have one like the present minister who is a staunch believer in free enterprise in the finance saddle in this country.
Not only would it be possible to make up for what it would cost to remove the 4 per cent floor, or to raise the exemption levels as has been suggested this afternoon by my colleague the member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin); not only could that be made up by an increase in corporation taxes or putting corporation taxes on a graduated basis, but I submit there is still room for a considerable increase in revenue if the Minister of Finance and his officials were to examine the whole basis of deductions that are allowed to those whose incomes are on a gross basis. Workers are in a very definite position. Their income is known, and when they have had it, they have had it. For the most part, the tax is deducted at the source, and if it is not all deducted there the chance of being able to claim any appreciable exemptions is on the whole rather slim. But those who earn an income that is described as gross, and who have the right to make deductions connected with the earning of that income, seem to be able to find a good many ways in which to claim deductions. In one

of the speeches which I made before-I shall not give it again-I gave figures from the United States as to the percentage of the various grades of income on which taxation is actually paid.
In connection with all this there recently appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune-it was on May 8 of this year-a news report which struck me as very significant. The story gave an account of a ruling given by Mr. R. S. Fordham of the income tax appeal board. Two Winnipeg gentlemen had appealed rulings of the Department of National Revenue, and had taken their cases to the income tax appeal board. These two gentlemen had cases that were more or less identical, so that to simplify the story I shall tell it in respect of just one of them.
This first appellant is a grocery broker and also the president of a company or a firm in Winnipeg. During two recent taxation years he made a fairly substantial sum of money on the side, and he made this money by buying conditional sales contracts from one of the finance corporations of the city of Winnipeg. The report said that this particular corporation was a little short on its bank credit, and wished to make a deal of this kind. This man, therefore, bought these conditional sales contracts and the result was that in the two years in question he made the sum of $12,503 on the side. Now, thinking of some of the interjections that are sometimes made from the other side of the house, that is not peanuts.
The income tax division of the Department of National Revenue regarded this as income, and insisted that this individual should pay income tax on this sum of $12,503 along with the tax that was to be paid on his other income. This particular individual felt that as the income tax law stood perhaps he could avoid paying a tax on this sum of money, so he appealed his case to the income tax appeal board. The Department of National Revenue was represented, of course, as was the appellant. The income tax appeal board ruled against the department and in favour of the appellant. The board ruled that this money which the man made on the side was to be considered as a capital gain, because it arose through a transaction which was not part of the regular business of the appellant. For that reason this individual was allowed to earn this $12,503 in two years without paying any income tax on it.
Part of what I have been saying is a paraphrased version of the report as it appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune. I wish to place on record a few words which I have taken from that report, and I may say that they
Income Tax Act
appeared in the newspaper report within quotation marks. The ruling of the board was to the effect that the reason the Department of National Revenue had tried to tax this man on this $12,503 was that its position, and I quote, "evidently arises from the erroneous belief, still prevalent in some quarters, that whenever a taxpayer makes a financial gain of any kind in a commercial transaction it must be viewed as income".
Now, Mr. Speaker, that is a comment which the average income tax payer would find very interesting. Most of us assume that whatever money people make is income so far as the income tax department is concerned. In this case may I say on behalf of the Minister of National Revenue and his department, that they thought this was income and that he should pay income tax on it. The income tax appeal board says not to go away with the opinion that every bit of money a man makes is income for the purposes of income tax. So in this case this individual was given the right by the income tax appeal board to earn this $12,503 on the side in two years without paying any income tax on it whatsoever. Mr. Speaker, anyone who is making $12,503 on the side is not making just $25 or $30 a week as his principal income. Undoubtedly he is up in a bracket were he is paying 50 per cent or 60 per cent on his income; and it is taxes of that order that this gentleman probably saved as a result of the ruling of the income tax appeal board.
I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, that it is not often that we get information of this kind, in these precise and specific terms. The newspaper reports even gave the gentleman's name, but I have not placed the name on the record. On a number of occasions I have tried to get the Income Tax Act amended so as to lift the veil of secrecy with regard to these matters, and hon. members will recall the difficulty I have had. In fact, my good friend the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) on one occasion called it peeping-Tom legislation. He did not like it.
I did not want the farmers to have all their business brought into the house.

We thought you were going to the farmers next.

there who are making this kind of money on the side and are not having to pay income tax on it? My suggestion is that if the law were tightened up in respect of sideline income made by people on gross incomes, there might be a considerable sum of money to be collected by the treasury.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yet he joins with me in my proposal that the 4 per cent floor under medical expenses should be wiped out. I do not agree with the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance that it would cost $48 million; but whatever it would cost, it is our responsibility on this side of the house to make some suggestions as to how that money might be made up. I suggest that here is one field where real money might be found. As 1 said a moment ago, a taxpayer of this kind is probably up in a 50 per cent or 60 per cent bracket. If we knew all the facts-if there was not the secrecy provision like an iron curtain around this kind of

information-we might find that there is really a substantial sum of money available in this way.
The minister said that it is a question of law. I am sure he knows what is coming. A few years ago, when the income tax appeal board on a question of law-pardon me, it was the exchequer court. It was before the income tax appeal board was set up to deal with these cases. The exchequer court, on a question of law, ruled that trade unionists were entitled to deductibility of their trade union dues. The government took the view that that was not the intention it had in its legislation and it immediately changed the law accordingly. As a matter of fact, it changed the legislation within a few weeks after the case was taken to the Exchequer Court of Canada. It did not even wait for the decision to be handed down. If the government feels that it has the right to step in and change the law when the courts have given an interpretation which suggests that the government's intention has not been carried out, then I suggest that it can be done in cases of this kind.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) or at least his department thought that the intention of the law was such as to cover these cases. Let me be fair to the income tax appeal board and say that the income tax appeal board said that it was a borderline case; at least they used language of that kind. It said that if the man went on making sums of money like this from this particular sideline, it would probably have to be counted as income in due course. The inference was that if he made money from different sidelines year in and year out, he could make money of this kind without being taxed on it.
As to interpreting the law, one threat which the government made some months ago has now been washed out. I refer to the Nolan case. The minister knows that when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) announced that this case was being taken to the privy council, he said that if the privy council ruled in a manner which was opposed to what the government's intention had been, they would bring in legislation to amend the law, so as to carry out the government's original intention. From the action of the Minister of National Revenue it would seem to me that in this case the government's intention was that this kind of income should be subject to tax. If the income tax appeal board has ruled, on a question of law, that the wording of the law is such that this kind of income is exempt, then I suggest that it is time for the law to be amended in respect of income of this kind.

1 urge that the minister go further than just tightening up the law to cover cases of the kind that the income tax appeal board has ruled on. I urge that he re-examine the whole question of the extent to which taxpayers on gross are able to claim deductions, the taxes on which must amount, during the course of the year, to many millions of dollars.
I come back again to what I said a moment ago. In the case of the ordinary worker, when he has had his income and has paid his tax, "he has had it". The deductions he can claim are few. He can claim his trade union dues now, thanks to the change that was made in the act last year. He can claim his donations to charity if he has receipts for them; but in many cases the contributions that a worker makes are not covered by receipts, and he does not get much relief in that way. He can claim his medical expenses if they are in excess of 4 per cent, not of his taxable income but of what amounts, in the case of the worker, to his gross income. That is just about all he can claim. He can make out his income tax return in half an hour. He pays taxes without question on his income. But in this other field, the field of gross income-if we could only get it all out; if there was not this veil of secrecy-I submit there is room for tremendous gain to the treasury.
I urge upon the minister that he do these two things that I have been talking about this afternoon. I urge that, on the one hand, he yet accede to the wish of parliament and of the people of Canada generally, and remove that 4 per cent floor under medical expenses deductible for income tax purposes. On the other hand I urge him to review the position of those who are on gross with respect to deductions that they are allowed, and in particular that sidelines such as those I have been speaking about in the Winnipeg case, with capital gains of that kind, should be subject to taxation.
Mr. Speaker, I do not often raise my voice in an income tax debate, for the reason that I am not an expert on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That does not deter others.

I know those who take part are professionals in the matter of income tax; but I wish to raise my voice only in a humble way in connection with one matter that has come to my attention through the years, and which I intended to discuss on previous occasions, but failed to do so.
I would direct the minister's attention particularly to small businesses in which perhaps only two or three persons are employed. I realize readily that the minister may have a
Income Tax Act
complete answer to the point I raise, and no doubt has given consideration to it much more fully than I have. For this reason I shall await his answer with interest.
These people, who might be described as the small fry in the business world, are in my opinion being discriminated against in the matter of income tax. Not only are they charged income tax, but they are asked by the government to be the chore boys of the Department of National Revenue. It is bad enough to ask them to be chore boys, but it is worse when they are asked to be chore boys without charge.
I understand that these people are ordered by the federal government to keep extra sets of books, and to figure the amounts which must be deducted, always having in mind the family status of the people working for them. Then the returns must be sent in, and they must be accurate. I am sure the minister knows that the people engaged in these small businesses do not have many dollars to give away. Most of them are having a difficult time to make ends meet. It seems to me that when they are asked by the federal government to shoulder this extra load on top of the burden they are now carrying; when they are asked to be the collection agency for the government, free of charge, some further consideration should be given to this aspect of the collection of income tax.
I do not proceed to argue the point with a closed mind. I am anxious to find out upon what basis the government has adopted its policy, and how it justifies its position; because when it asks someone to do a job the person who does the job makes sure the government pays for it. This would seem to be the only instance where the federal government insists upon the work being done free of charge.
I have no doubt the minister will say that huge corporations and big business should not be relieved of this responsibility. He will point out that if we relieve the little fellow we must include the richer man. Those people in the upper brackets, so far as I am concerned, can speak for themselves. It is the little fellow who has to have someone in the House of Commons who will speak for him. He speaks to his member of parliament and others in the neighbourhood, and naturally comes to the conclusion that he should not have to bear this extra load.
I am not in a critical mood, but I am anxious to have the government consider what I have said. If it can be shown that my presentation lacks merit, I shall be the first to admit it. I do think, however, that there is a case to be made for the little fellow

Income Tax Act
who has done work for the government without charge. An examination of the public accounts would seem to show that he is the only one working for nothing, and I suggest he should not be discriminated against in this way.
When the minister replies he may have a satisfactory answer because, after all, the problem is to place the burden as equitably as possible. I think, however, most hon. members will be struck by what would appear to be an injustice against those having small earning capacity, who have to shoulder all this bookkeeping and accounting work at the request-and, may I say, more than the request; the order-of the federal Department of National Revenue.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw again to the minister's attention the matter of compensation paid to farmers in Saskatchewan for animals destroyed as the result of the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak. When the matter was before the house in March I asked that the compensation so paid be exempt from income tax, because this is not really a form of income in the regular sense. Many farmers will have lost their means of livelihood for the next few years, or until such time as they can build up other herds. On the earlier occasion the minister listened sympathetically to what I had to say, and said he would give the matter further consideration. I would ask him to give us any information he may have, when he speaks.

Mr. Speaker, in a general way it is my opinion, and so far as I can gather it is the opinion of my constituents, that the income tax structure is now far too high. It is time something was done to relieve the great majority of people-I would say probably 85 per cent of them-who are in the lower income tax brackets.
The vast majority of Canadian people are being progressively impoverished, and this at a time when the Liberals are pleased to tell us that we are more prosperous than ever before in our history. How anyone can put those two facts together and make sense out of them is beyond my understanding; because the prosperity of the people certainly depends not only upon the amount of money they obtain but also upon the amount they are able to keep and to use, either for saving or spending, for what they consider to be the needs of life.
Why should the people of Canada be penalized more severely, the more goods and services they produce? It is forecast that in the present year in the neighbourhood of $23 billion worth of goods will be produced

in Canada. No hon. member in the House of Commons, and few people throughout the country, will fail to realize that the amount of goods and services we produce constitutes the real acquisition of wealth of the nation, and should be the basis upon which to determine our prosperity, our well-being as a nation, or lack of it.
If we have reached the point where we are producing $23 billion worth of goods a year, why should something like 85 per cent of all the people in the country be absolutely at their wits' end to know how to get along? Why are they literally groaning with anxiety for fear they may not be able to get along? Setting aside all theories of income tax and all that sort of thing, all theories of revenue, we are faced with this bald, simple and easily understandable fact which I submit ought to be taken cognizance of by every responsible person in this nation.
It is commonly said by a good many people, and was repeated in this house during world war II, that whatever is physically possible ought to be financially possible. That is, the more physical well-being a nation can produce, the more financial well-being it should be able to enjoy. May I submit that the system' the minister is following under this bill does not make financially possible what is physically possible. As a matter of fact, many of the imposts which are being levied under this bill are of such a nature in their incidence that they actually tend to discourage production in the nation because they take away from so large a percentage of the people the very income they need to buy the goods industry can produce, thereby destroying automatically the market for the industry. Take the case of the cheese producers, to name only one of hundreds. Thus they tend to destroy production in this land of probably first-rate abundance, potentially. That is another matter which I think needs to be considered.
I do not suppose the minister will take the trouble to state whether he believes that what is physically possible ought to be financially possible. If he does believe that, then the only logical thing he can do is realign his whole system of raising money in this country. I just wished to raise that matter in passing.
I look with great alarm upon the increase of taxes in this nation. As far as I can see, if these taxes continue to increase as they have Canadians might just as well bid good-bye to freedom. If a man cannot have an income and have a little of it left that he himself can dispose of, I ask you in the name of common sense how you can say he has any freedom at all. The very things the hon. member for

Peel (Mr. Graydon) mentioned a few minutes ago are cases in point. If the government can say to a man running a little business and having the greatest difficulty making a living, "you have to do thus and so and thus and so and thus and so," and as a result of all those "thuses" and "so's" it costs the man, $150 extra for services in having his income tax returns made out, for doing the government's "chore-boy" work, as the hon. member well called it, for which he gets no return, you have to stretch your concept of freedom a long way to look upon that man as having any freedom in respect of the running of his affairs. So it is all through the economy as far as I can see.
It will be said that we have to have money. The minister will probably say that we are calling for bigger and better old age pensions, for bigger and better family allowances and so on, and that we have to have the money. I agree that we have to have the money, but my contention is that we do not have to get the money by stealing every dollar of it from the people's pockets. That is just where the moaning cry a few minutes ago of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) is shown to be so hopeless. He says you cannot get money anywhere except by taking it out of the people's pockets; that when you have all there is in their pockets, you might just as well give up; it does not matter how rich your country is or how many things you can produce in the way of goods and services, you just cannot go any further; what is physically possible is not in his thinking financially possible, and that is the end of it.
I maintain that is a completely unrealistic attitude to take toward the whole business of financing our country at this time. It is well known, and I do not need to repeat it here, that I have argued time and time again in this house that under appropriate circumstances when there is adequate production in the country, adequate supplies, money can be created by the state debt-free and used for the benefit of the people of Canada. Up to the present time no argument has been adduced in this house to disprove my position. I maintain that no argument can be adduced by anybody in this house to disprove my position.
That is going a little bit too far.

I challenge the hon. member to take the floor the first time he gets a chance. There will be no more left of him than was left of the prairie chicken by the time the gatling gun got through with it. As we go into these trying times, and they are terribly trying,
Income Tax Act
why not give thought to this all-important consideration? Why tax our people to the point where they are disheartened and bewildered and wondering whether they have a friend in the world? Why drive them to that position? Why not realize that by the adoption of proper measures, what is physically possible actually can be made financially possible. That certainly cannot be done by taxation.
This is the general statement I wish to make. I do not intend to argue at length, but I am sure that in speaking as I am now I am voicing the opinion, at least the desire, of no fewer than 85 per cent of all Canadian people.
Just one more little thing needs to be said and I shall close. The minister will say, "What you are proposing will bring inflation." Let me ask hon. members on all sides of the house to take the definition which the hon. member for Greenwood gave us a year ago, and which is a good one, as to the cause of inflation; namely, that it occurs when "we have too many dollars chasing too few goods". Is there any conceivable reason why in Canada you cannot have so many goods that you could not get enough dollars chasing them to cause inflation? I ask hon. members to go through the whole list of our products: potatoes, vegetables, fruits, fuel, dairy products, poultry products, livestock products, grain products. Is there any possibility of reasoning that under normal conditions Canada could not produce so many of at least 90 per cent of those products that no matter how much money the people had in their pockets there would not be enough money "chasing those goods" to cause a rise in price?
If the minister is afraid to use the device I have urged upon him because there would be danger of inflation, then let me say that it is all-important that he adopt such measures as will increase the production in Canada of any commodity in connection with which he thinks there is any danger of a serious shortage of supply developing.
I doubt very much if the minister can show that he has conscientiously taken any steps to increase the production of any commodity. The other day we did take steps to increase the production of gold. I wonder if the minister can point to any other single commodity produced in Canada in respect of which we are taking similar steps to increase production. If we were to take steps as striking, as palpable in connection with the production of anything else in Canada as those we are taking in connection with gold production we should get a production increase almost beyond our capacity to contain. Why not try it where necessary?

Income Tax Act
When we have supply in Canada up to a point where we can feel positive there is no danger of a shortage developing with a consequent rise in price through scarcity, why not use this device of state-created debt-free dollars which I have been suggesting? I close by saying once more that in my judgment the income tax is far, far too high. I did not say very much about excise taxes. I felt like saying something then, but I thought what I had to say would be more appropriate on this bill. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity of speaking as I have spoken.
I want to ask a few questions for my own information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will be very brief. One or two points were raised in the course of the debate concerning which I want to say a word, particularly the question of the allowance for medical expenses. I have already said what I am going to say, but in view of the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I feel I must repeat it. I feel deeply that it is a fundamental principle of our Income Tax Act that no expense which is an ordinary living expense should be paid out of income before tax. I happen to know that view is fully shared by my predecessor who introduced this measure. That is the reason I have been unable to bring myself to conscientiously recommend to parliament and to the country that this particular type of ordinary living expense, which unfortunately because of human frailty is an expense that sooner or later is incurred by every person in the country, should be wholly deductible from income before tax.
When the measure was introduced early in the war a figure of 5 per cent was suggested, after investigation, as representing what the average family spent for medical, dental and allied expenses. In order to mitigate the hardship of excessive medical expenses, provision was made that expenses in excess of 5 per cent should be deductible, with certain ceilings which were necessary for obvious reasons

to prevent wealthy people getting undue benefit. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, that was lowered in 1944 from 5 to 4 per cent primarily to take care of expenditures for drugs which for administrative reasons it was difficult to include in the exemptions.
I do not say that it is, but it may be that the 4 per cent ceiling is too high. Perhaps it should be reduced. I considered that in the budget consideration, but I came to the conclusion that it was not. However, I did come to the conclusion that in the light of changed circumstances the ceilings might properly be raised. While I followed the direction of the house to consider the elimination of the floor and to allow all medical expenses to be deductible, those were the reasons I could not, as I have said, conscientiously recommend that course to the house and to the country.
Responsibility, Mr. Speaker, is a sobering experience. If others had had the experience that I have had of being Minister of Finance charged with the responsibility of raising very large sums of money and endeavouring to the best of my ability to spread the burden as fairly as possible over the taxpayers of Canada, I think they would come to the same conclusion I did. Some reference was made to by-elections. I put that view forward at a public meeting at the city of Kitchener in the constituency of Waterloo North, and that was one of the by-elections in which the Liberal candidate was successful.
I would not crow too much over that one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am stating it as a fact. I have repeated why I think it would be unsound, unfair and unjust to eliminate the floor with respect to medical expenses. Other points were raised in the course of this discussion but I think it might be more convenient if I were to deal with them when we are in committee. Members can then ask specific questions as to the points they have in mind.

government. What I am particularly concerned about is the expression "at arms' length". I should like the minister to outline what that term really means. Does it mean I cannot sell a business or property to my son or my brother?
Your uncle or your aunt.

I suppose what constitutes
payment depends upon the law of the particular province in which the loan is entered into, but I would not think the giving of a note, which would simply be the extension or renewal of a loan, would constitute payment within the meaning of the statute. I appreciate what the minister has said, but I am wondering whether in fact there has been
Income Tax Act
sufficient experience in connection with the act so that precedents have been established which can be ascertained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate this is a new provision which is extending the operation of the section. It is a relaxing measure. It is permitting loans to be made which up to the present time have not been permitted. We have to be pretty careful about it because it could be abused, and that is why this provision is put in here.

On that same question, a shareholder gets a loan from the company. What difference does it make whether it is paid back that year, the year after or the year after that? There must be some instances where that would work great hardship, actually.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be the simplest way to avoid ever paying dividends. In the case of a company, as my hon. friend knows, when dividends are paid they attract taxes in the hands of the recipient, personal income tax. If there was no provision such as this in the act it would be the simplest way to avoid ever making a distribution of profits which should be subject to personal income tax.

I quite appreciate that, and I quite agree with the motive that prompts that section of the legislation. But there must be cases from time to time where a genuine hardship is worked on that same basis, because after all the income tax department must, on numerous occasions, benefit very greatly at the expense of the individual taxpayer, and sometimes in what would seem to be almost a discriminatory way. I should think there must be some way legislation could be framed so that if the taxpayer did not pay the loan back, or part of it in any event during that current year, it could be paid back in another year without working the hardship that would seem to be imposed on the taxpayer in this instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

As my hon. friend will recall, being a legal man, this is a section that has been in the Income Tax Act and the preceding act for a great many years. Formerly it prohibited loans to shareholders, with virtually no exception. That has been successively relaxed. This represents the last relaxation, and for the good reasons I indicated to the hon. member for Greenwood it has to be hedged about with some considerable safeguards. This section now permits a loan to be made for any purpose, provided it is repaid within one year from the end of the fiscal period of the corporation out

Income Tax Act
of which the loan is made, that is the following fiscal year. So if it were made at the beginning of one fiscal'year the maximum period allowed for repayment would be two years. If it were made at the end it would only be twelve months. That I think is a pretty generous revision. The original act said no loans to shareholders at all. The companies which are not in the lending business are not supposed to be lending money. If a man wants to borrow money, under ordinary circumstances he goes to a lending institution, the bank. In other words, loans are not to be used as a vehicle for getting dividends out without paying income tax.

Will the
minister not agree that there are other alternatives-

Can the minister tell us what the official position is with respect to compensation paid to farmers in Saskatchewan on account of the foot-and-mouth disease?

The payment to which my hon. friend refers is of course the annual payment. It refers to payment year after year.

I understand it is perhaps universal now that an individual who is a member of an approved plan gets an exemption on the payments he makes from time to time. On the other hand when he receives his annuity, that is taxable. There are still cases, I believe, where it may be paid in a lump sum, and my understanding is that in those cases the lump sum may be spread over three years. Am I right in that?

Then do I understand that the question I have raised is really academic, because no man could ever be put in that position? Is that a characteristic of the plan, that he may always choose an annuity, so the three-year difficulty would not arise?
