speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Subsection 2 of section 3 relates to the amendment that was first enacted last year concerning the deductibility of trade union dues, and this amendment would include payments made by workers covered by what is known as the Rand formula. I should like to ask the minister whether consideration has been given to making any other what might be called administrative changes in connection with this provision. As the minister knows, the deductibility of trade union dues was a most welcome provision. He has had experience before with some of the things he has introduced being welcomed, but at the same time those who are affected can see room for improvement. In this particular case I find a number of trade unionists are concerned over the complicated nature of the formula that applies to these deductions.
The complication arises out of two main facts. On the one hand it arises from the fact that payments for trade union purposes generally and payments into trade union pension plans, where such plans are approved, are covered separately. In other words they are covered in separate sections of the act. In the end it amounts to the same thing in dollars and cents, but it is very complicated for trade union secretaries particularly to have to issue two separate receipts, and to break down the dues that are paid in a lump sum as between those that are for trade union purposes generally and those that may be for a pension plan. I would point out that at the moment I am talking only about such pension plans as are approved. There are same trade union pension plans, in addition to the supplementary one in Toronto about which I have talked to the minister so often, which have not yet been approved. At the moment I am saying that the division between the two creates complexities.
The other complication is created by virtue of the wording further on in the section we are now amending, which says that one cannot claim this deduction for any purpose not directly related to the ordinary operating expenses of the association or trade union to which they were paid. This means that many unions have quite a time determining just what percentage of the dues that are paid

Income Tax Act
comes under this provision. For example, I am told that if a trade union is renting office premises, the rent that it has to pay is regarded as part of the operating expenses and therefore the amounts paid by members thereto are allowed. On the other hand, I am told that if a trade union is setting aside money to build or purchase its own building, that is regarded in a different light and is not allowed. Similarly, what are sometimes called defence funds are not allowed. In some cases they might amount to quite a bit, but in most cases they do not amount to very much in terms of tax saving.
I can speak with some knowledge on this matter because I happen to belong to a trade union that is affected. The union to which I belong has a pension plan which is approved. If I were to read the minister the formula that has been sent out to the secretaries of the locals across the country for working this out, he would admit it is rather complicated. This complication arises from two facts. The first is the distinction between pension payments and ordinary payments, and the other is that of knowing what expenses of the union are allowed. I wonder if consideration could not be given to combining the two payments into one, at least where the pension plan has been approved. My other suggestion is this. Would it not be possible to simplify the whole matter by making it possible for the whole of the trade union dues to be deducted? If the minister wants to put some kind of limitation on that, something in the nature of a ceiling, I suggest it would be a lot simpler if he were to base it on a percentage of the taxpayer's income rather than in the terms I have already described.
There is one other question I should like to ask. Would it not be possible to arrange for the T-4 slips, particularly in a case where the Rand formula or some other form of union security is in effect, to show these deductions and simplify the work of the secretary of the union concerned?

speechtext: I understand that the questions raised by the hon. member are now under consideration in the department. Every time we add one of these exemptions from income it does complicate the preparation and filing of returns, both by the taxpayer and by the tax department, but that is probably unavoidable.

Where a taxpayer's chief source of income for a taxation year is neither farming-[DOT]

The Alberta Social Credit government has not sold one foot of any resource in that province since it came into power in 1935, not a single foot. The hon. member for Vegreville knows that what I say is the truth. I was a member of the provincial cabinet from 1935 to 1945, and I know. I was there and helped to lay down the policy. We sent Mr. Tanner, the minister of lands and mines, over to Britain to see everybody he could see over there, and invite the British people to spend their money in Alberta. They did nothing. Since the British people have lost their Iranian oil fields, they have been looking down their noses and have wished they had come in. They wish they had the vision that other people had.

Boundary Pipeline Corporation credit there is for the development of those resources. They are getting a decent run for their money, and they are secure. But when they did come in to risk their capital in the development of these resources, they did not buy a single foot of anything. They bought and paid a very heavy price for, first, the privilege of exploration over a wide area. After they had satisfied themselves in their exploratory efforts, then they were given, for a price, the right to select an area they could develop. They were given a lease on that area and nothing else, a lease which could be revoked at any time if the company did not fulfil every jot and tittle of the terms of the agreement.
The ownership of these resources stayed, and still remains, in the hands of the Alberta government. After the development took place, if the companies found oil or gas they began immediately to pay a top royalty to the government of the province. The starting point-at least when I had anything to do with the policy-was around 12J per cent. It has been raised now until the average over the province is 14-1 per cent. The ownership of these resources remains in the crown, in the hands of the people of the province of Alberta. The rates for leases or royalties or rentals can be adjusted at any time after due notice has been given of that intention by the government of the province. At various times the government has made such adjustments in the rentals, royalty rates and so on.
These resources are, therefore, still in the hands of Alberta, and they have not been sold out to anybody. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This is the section that relates to the deduction for medical expenses. It provides one or two changes from the basis previously in existence, notably in that it raises the ceiling in two respects, and also makes a slight change in the wording of the preliminary part.
The wording as it now stands requires that, in order to be deductible, medical expenses must be both incurred and paid within a twelve month period ending in the taxation year. From now on it will be possible to claim those expenses, even though they are only paid within such a twelve months period. That change is a welcome one. It does not solve some of the problems I have suggested from time to time, particularly in the case of those who are faced with bills so heavy that it might take them two or three years to pay them off. Nevertheless this is some improvement and, because it is in that direction, it is helpful.
However, while I am on this section I feel I should say a few more words concerning the refusal of the minister to consider at this session the removal of the 4 per cent floor. This afternoon during the debate on second reading he indicated that he had considered the matter again, after my motion of March 26 was passed by the house, but he still felt that he could not conscientiously recommend the abolition of this provision. I believe I am representing faithfully what he said if I say he bases his position with respect to the removal of the floor on the ground that 4 per cent of one's income is the ordinary or average amount a taxpayer spends on medical expenses. If that is so, I take it that it is his contention that there is no great advantage in providing relief to everyone which, in turn, has to be made up by charging those same people taxation in some other form so as to make up for the relief given.
The fallacy in the minister's position is that it is based on the concept of averages. It is one thing to say that the people of Canada spend on an average 4 per cent of their incomes on medical expenses, but it is quite a

Income Tax Act
different thing to say that makes it an ordinary amount which everyone in Canada is paying. If the minister could claim that 4 per cent of one's income is an amount everyone actually pays, then I would say there is some point in his argument. He could claim that since everyone pays 4 per cent of income for medical expenses, the fair thing would be to provide tax relief for those who have to pay more than that floor which everyone has paid. But this 4 per cent figure trotted out as the average amount that people spend is not a floor; it is only an average.
There are many fortunate people in Canada who in the course of a year get by without spending as much as 4 per cent of their income on medical expenses. There will be some extremely fortunate people who get by in a year without spending anything on medical expenses. It may be that those who are fortunate one year will not be so fortunate another year. Part of what the minister said is correct, namely that medical expenses sooner or later catch up with all of us, but not every one of us every year. Again, thinking of all of us, in our lives as a whole, there is an average amount paid. But no one is right at that average point. And it is because of the wide variation between those who have to spend nothing at all on medical expenses and those who are called upon to spend large amounts, that it seems to me the 4 per cent figure for deductibility is unfair.
The minister may say I have admitted that those who are fortunate enough in one year not to have medical expenses do have them in another year. All right; let the income tax arrangements provide relief in the years when one does have medical expenses, and let the taxpayer forgo any such relief in the years when he is fortunate enough not to have those expenses.
There are other aspects of the matter I could discuss, but since we have brought this matter to the attention of the minister time and again, I shall not go into it at greater length this evening. In a sentence or two I would urge that the minister should remember that his definition of medical expenses does not include many things entering into the cost of an illness. That is another reason why, with that restricted definition, I feel there should be no floor at all. But the main basis upon which some of us rest our case for the abolition of the 4 per cent floor is as I have stated, that the 4 per cent figure the minister is using is merely an average; it is not a floor.
What one must consider is that people have these tremendous variations. I hope the minister will even yet reconsider this

position and make some change. I feel so strongly that the floor should be abolished altogether that I dislike suggesting any compromise by way of reducing it; but I would rather see it at, let us say, 3 per cent, 2 per cent or 1 per cent than to remain at 4 per cent. At any rate I still hope the minister will do something about the matter at this stage.

Mr. Chairman, as I have said on former occasions, I too feel that the floor should have been abolished. I was interested this afternoon in the minister's remarks. I feel he is sincere in his contention that a certain floor is equivalent to ordinary expenses, or what he calls ordinary living expenses.

speechtext: Medical expenses.

The minister called it ordinary living expenses. I feel there is a point that has probably been overlooked right along. Wherever you have even small expenses with regard to illness there are always extraordinary expenses to be met in the home. Those expenses cannot be called ordinary living expenses. They may be due to the need of extra help, to the necessity of buying luxury foods in order to tempt the ill person to eat, or they may be due to the necessity of travelling to the hospital or wherever the ill person may be. I contend; as I have contended previously, that these expenses amount to far more than the 4 per cent of income which the minister contends is reasonable for the average taxpayer to assume for medical expenses.
I do not wish to belabour this point because I have spoken on it on several occasions and I am sure the committee is quite familiar with my views; but in proposing the amendments to the act I think the minister might very well have made 26 (b) read, "an amount equal to the medical expenses paid either by the taxpayer or by his legal representative."
Most of us are faced with ordinary medical expenses, and I think we all realize that when severe medical expenses must be met any concession is of value. I urge the minister now, as I have on previous occasions, to reconsider this matter carefully and take into consideration the fact that in the last few years living costs have advanced to the point where former considerations are no longer current. We have passed from the era of a few years ago when taxes were low, when exemptions were higher and when the average family faced with illness did not have to contend with the high cost of the services rendered or of the medical supplies that might have to be procured. Under these circumstances I feel that despite the hours that have been spent

on this point by the committee, and I am sure also by the department, too little consideration has been given to it.
There is another point in connection with section 7 to which I should like to speak at this time. This was referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Calgary East. I refer to the employment of full-time help in a home where illness occurs. This is covered by section 26 (b) (iv) and (v) where deductions are allowed for the expense of employing a full-time attendant for persons who are ill or who are totally disabled or blind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose my hon. friend is aware of section 26 (b) (iv)?

I have not yet reached the point. I am making a comparison between the home which has lost its housekeeper, let us say, either through illness of the housekeeper herself or through her employment in order to earn a livelihood for her family because of the illness of the normal breadwinner in the home. The government has recognized that under certain circumstances deductions should be allowed for the cost of a full-time attendant for a person necessarily confined by reason of illness, injury or affliction to a bed or wheelchair. Then in the next paragraph reference is made to the remuneration for a full-time attendant upon a taxpayer who is totally blind.
That being so, the government should also give consideration to the household which has been deprived of the person who normally keeps house and takes care of the children in that home, either by reason of the illness of that person or the illness of the breadwinner in that home as a result of which the normal homemaker is obliged to seek some sort of employment which will provide her with the means of sustaining her family.
For that reason I support the contention which has been put forward in this committee, especially this afternoon by the hon. member for Calgary East, that a deduction should be allowed for the remuneration of one fulltime attendant required under these circumstances.

Mr. Chairman, I find myself in full agreement with the hon. member for Hamilton West and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I do not wish to delay the committee because I have mentioned this matter before. I urge the Minister of Finance and the government to reconsider their position on this matter. I cannot understand their attitude with reference to it. I think it will be admitted that the whole committee is in favour of the elimination of this floor.
Income Tax Act
In these days when we are talking about social welfare, the welfare state, the necessity of doing so much for so many, surely this exemption is highly justified. If an hon. member wishes to contribute to a hospital he may deduct that contribution for income tax purposes. We are talking about establishing health programs and so on, and I do submit that the cost of illness within the family should be exempt from income tax. I do not think there should be a floor under that exemption.
I am sure we all know of many families who have suffered terrific losses. We must know of young men and young women with small families who have had their plans interrupted, who have had' to give up business enterprises, who have been stalled and stymied, who have had their whole lives changed because the wife or husband has been seriously impaired by illness. As the hon. member for Hamilton West says, it is not only the cost of the illness that bears so heavily, it is the complications that are involved in such illness. I would go even further and say that any person who is generous enough to contribute toward the cost of illness in another family is just as much entitled to exemption for income tax purposes with respect to such payment as if he had made a contribution to a hospital. Therefore I urge that the Minister of Finance reconsider his position. I know he is a sympathetic and kindly natured gentleman.
Be careful.
The elections are over now.

One of his supporters says the elections are over. They are not over yet. There will be more coming, and some important ones. Coming events cast their shadows before, and if you started to dream last night about the future you should have seen shadows of dangers to come unless you listen to the opposition, which evidently is more popular than you are at the present time. I do not want to embarrass the government. If I had been here last night I might have been impelled to embarrass them, but tonight I feel there is always a calm after the storm. I have seen the hilarious attitude of government supporters when they won one by-election, but they will observe the Conservative quiet when we win four or five.
You should have been here at three o'clock today.

I am not disturbed by these rumblings. They are the anguish of pain rather than rejoicing. I am not going to chide the Minister of Finance about his misfortunes. He knows them better than I do, but in all

Income Tax Act
seriousness I urge the government to reconsider their position with respect to this matter. Like every other hon. member, no matter how long or short a time he has been in the house, I have had experience with the troubles of our constituents. Whether or not they are our supporters they come to us if we are in public life, and we sympathize with those who suffer from illness. I say again that I cannot see why the cost of illness should not be exempt from income tax without a floor. I think of labouring men who have been embarrassed by having to accept assistance from municipalities, women who have had cancer, children who have had tuberculosis, children with infantile paralysis.
Strange as it may seem, unfortunately I believe it is a fact that the percentage of illness is greater among those who can least afford it financially. I feel that if the Minister of Finance wished to help some unfortunate family in Dufferin-Simcoe his contribution should be exempt from income tax just as much as if he made a contribution to a hospital in Montreal, or a hospital in Toronto. I think it is only sound, and I urge in all sincerity that the minister reconsider his position. He is aware of the support this proposal has had from all corners of the house. If a proposal for health insurance or a welfare state has anything except a popular appeal for political purposes, then surely the exemption of contributions to the cost of illness is merited in the case of those who may wish to assist not only their own families but, if they are fortunate to have no illness in their own families, to assist other families. I think it should be carried that far. It should be just as legitimate and sound to exempt such contributions from income tax as if a person gave $5,000 to a hospital, for which he is exempted from income tax.
I am not going to detain the committee further except to say that to my mind the proposal is sound from every angle. From the way the house supported the resolution before it earlier in the session, I believe it is wholeheartedly in favour of the proposal. Therefore I urge the Minister of Finance to reconsider his position not because there is any political aspect to this proposal but because it has a sympathetic touch, economic soundness and humanitarian logic that no one can deny.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is not very much I can add to what I said this afternoon, but I was interested to hear my hon. friend say that he supported the proposals made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Knowing his views I was particularly surprised,

because the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre quite properly said that when one suggests a loss of revenue, in this case of from $48 million to $50 million, one should suggest an alternative means of raising it, and he suggested an increase in the corporation income taxes. I was not quite clear whether my hon. friend was supporting that portion of the suggestion.
He endorsed it in full.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think he endorsed it in full.

I might add that I happen to be the head of a little corporation from which the government now takes 56-4 per cent, and there is very little left. However, I will quite readily agree to take as much more as is needed to make up the balance in order to help people who are ill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wonder if my hon. friend's directors would confirm that statement.
I submit that the minister has yet to substantiate his claim that it will cost $48 million to $50 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is one matter I should raise in answer to a point brought up by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. The proposal to entirely exempt medical expenses from income tax only gives relief to income tax payers so far as medical expenses are concerned. There are a great many wage earners in this country who, by reason of marital exemption and so on, do not pay any income tax. I think it is quite proper that a wealthy man like the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe should make a contribution to the Toronto hospital and that I should make a more modest one to the Montreal hospital in order to assist those people in our communities who, by reason of lack of income, are not able to pay their medical expenses, and who perhaps are not income tax payers.

Thanks for the compliment.
I did not have enough left to contribute to them.
Following the line of argument the minister has just advanced, the very fact that there are a great many wage earners in Canada, who, because they do not pay income tax-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: About half of them.

-would not derive any benefit from the abolition of the 4 per cent floor, is in my opinion no good reason for retaining it for those who do pay income tax. The reason that half the people in Canada today have no health insurance and no protection against sickness is that the Liberal

government, which has been promising health insurance since 1919, has failed to keep its promise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do we have to debate health insurance tonight, Mr. Chairman?

Because of that fact the people of Canada today have no protection against sickness. That being the case, I would say it is all the more argument why the minister should relent with respect to the position he has taken. As the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe pointed out, it is granted that the minister may lose a few million dollars, but we in this group have pointed out how the minister can make up that loss.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You have the support of Dufferin-Simcoe now, too.
And the hon. member for Moose Jaw.

The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has offered the minister an alternative. He has said that as far as he is concerned he is quite willing to support higher taxation of corporations in order to offset the revenue-
How naive can you be?

-that would be wiped out by the elimination of the 4 per cent floor on medical expenses. What is more important, if the minister refuses to wipe out the whole 4 per cent I would urge that he at least consider a compromise. A man in the $3,000 income bracket must have a medical bill of $120 before he can get any relief at all. A man in the $2,000 income bracket must have $80. That is about as much as the ordinary working class people can ever afford for health and medical bills. If their bills are larger than that they will have to go into debt or go without medical service. They will have to keep away from the hospital when they need it. Even a reduction of 2 per cent would be some relief.
Then there is this further point. I doubt whether any measure that has ever come before this parliament has had more popular support throughout the country than the motion which this house unanimously adopted to eliminate the 4 per cent clause. These are the people who are concerned. The people who pay the taxes are quite ready to see that 4 per cent wiped out. I urge the minister to let this clause stand for the time being and give it further consideration. If he is not willing to wipe out the entire 4 per cent, then compromise and wipe out 2 per cent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was hoping that a little further thought might result in the minister changing his mind. After all, some progress has been made. He did get the support of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe in connection with the proposal I made. Surely the minister should not expect everybody else to make moves and for him to make no move at all. The house expressed its view on this matter on my motion of March 26. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe is prepared to pay more taxes to make up any extra cost, and I suggest in all seriousness that this indicates the attitude of people generally toward this whole problem.
I indicated when I was on my feet earlier that I feel so strongly the floor should be wiped out altogether that I hesitate to suggest a compromise. But I said before, and my colleague the hon. member for York South has repeated it, that if the minister is not prepared to go all the way and wipe out the floor, surely he should reconsider reducing it to 2 per cent, or to a nominal figure of 1 per cent. I admit if he did that I would introduce a motion next year to wipe that out, but it would be progress in the right direction. If he is not prepared to consider that compromise may I ask him to consider another one that was sent to him-at least, I trust it came to his attention-from the Windsor chamber of commerce. That body on May 13, 1952, addressed a letter which I believe was sent to all members of parliament, in which they enclosed copies of a number of resolutions on taxation matters, and one of them related to this question of the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes.
The specific suggestion made by the Windsor chamber of commerce was that the 4 per cent relate not to the total income of the taxpayer but to the taxable income. The minister realizes that this would lower the basic amount that the 4 per cent would produce, because the $3,000 taxpayer, to whom my colleague the hon. member for York South was just referring, must at the present time spend $120 before he starts to get any benefit from it. If on the other hand he was a married man with $2,000 exemption his taxable income would be $1,000 and 4 per cent of that would be $40. As a matter of fact, in the resolution submitted by the Windsor chamber of commerce a couple of examples were worked out, showing that such a change would be of greater benefit to those in the lower brackets. Those in the lower brackets in many instances would

Income Tax Act
find their position improved doubly; whereas those in the upper brackets would find the relative improvement much less.
I can say with respect to that the same as I said with respect to lowering the floor to 2 per cent or 1 per cent, namely that it is only a compromise. It is, however, a move in the direction of wiping out the floor altogether, and I very strongly feel that should be done. But I wonder if as a compromise the minister has considered either of those proposals: reducing the floor to a lower percentage, or the proposal contained in the resolution of the Windsor chamber of commerce which was addressed to the Minister of Finance and, I presume, submitted to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I considered those proposals and, as I indicated this afternoon, I considered whether the 4 per cent figure should be lower, but I came to the conclusion that it should not be at this time. The proposals which are made in this section that is now before the committee represent the maximum which I am prepared to recommend at this time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Will the minister comment on the point raised by the Windsor chamber of commerce?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is exactly the same proposal that is made by the hon. member for York South. In effect it is reducing the 4 per cent, and the principle on which the 4 per cent is based is that it represents the average expenditure by a person of his total income on medical expenses. And as I said before, the principle on which this section is based is that no ordinary expenditures should be paid out of income before taxes. It is only exceptional or unusual expenses, and the logic and the reason behind the provision in the act is that it is only expenditures that are in excess of this national average that are unusual or exceptional medical expenses.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

On section 8-Dividends not deductible.
Clause 8 is highly technical. I wonder whether the minister will explain in a general way what is behind the deduction and also refer to the limitations that are introduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are a number of subsections here which relate to different matters, as the explanatory note indicates. The first, that is subsection 1, is a relieving provision. It extends the provisions under which a corporation receiving dividends from another corporation may deduct such dividends in computing taxable income to include dividends from certain foreign business corporations. There are not very many of these, but the situation needed correcting. I shall ask to have an amendment moved in a moment to make part of the section effective from 1950. As I say, it is a relieving section. We have had representations from tax foundations and others that this should be made effective from 1950, when the section first came into force. We have looked into it. We feel sure there can be no possibility of abuse, and before the section passes I shall ask that these subsections be made applicable from 1950.
The subsections referred to relate to the block provision which was inserted in the act when we enacted section 95 (a) permitting the payment of a 15 per cent rate on accumulated surplus, and was put there in order to prevent the transfer of surplus of one corporation to another corporation and thereby avoid the payment of tax on this accumulation.
These subsections, which are long and rather technical, are intended, as the explanatory note explains, to clear up an anomaly in the present law where shares of a company have rights to dividends upon winding up which differ from those existing prior to winding up. It is to take care of shares nominally known as class A, class B or some other type of share, which has different rights, depending upon whether distribution is made while the company is in existence or whether distribution is made when the company is being wound up.
I am reminded that the hon. member asked for this or a similar provision last year. I told him that consideration would be given to it, and the officers of my department have studied the matter in the meantime. This long and rather involved section is the result of that examination. The main section, as the committee appreciates, is a loophole section. It is a section to prevent the avoidance of tax, but these amendments are to

make sure that in certain special cases such as I have indicated, there will not be any unfair operation of the section.
In the last subsection-

On section 18-Armed forces regulations.
How is this section actually going to work out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is the new system of taxation with respect to the armed forces which was introduced last year. The committee will recall that, speaking very generally, the pay and allowances of the armed forces were considered as though they were completely separate income from anything else. Provisions were worked out with allowances for charitable deductions and so on, deductions were established, and a soldier had no further obligation to file any income tax return. The system has been well liked by the armed forces, but as the legal members in the committee will appreciate there were some very serious technical difficulties involved. The officials of national revenue, the armed forces and my department have been trying to get this system codified, but frankly up to the present time we have not been able to do it.
This section gives a discretionary power to establish regulations setting out these details. The alternative would have been to abandon the privilege entirely, which no one wanted to do. The section sets out the principles upon which the tax is to be assessed. The regulations, which I hope we shall have ready within the next month or two though

I shall not make any firm promise on that, will be tabled and published as soon as they are available. I would propose to incorporate the rules which are set out in these regulations in the act next year when they are ready. This is an interim provision to enable the system to be carried on this year until we can work out the full details of the system. The principles are well established, but there are so many quirks that we have not been able to get them all spelled out in detail.

On section 25-Application of part to crown corporations.

Will the minister explain the meaning of the new section 25 of the Income Tax Act? I presume that is the provision to help certain public utility companies. There seems to be some uncertainty as to what effect that will have in so far as the general public are concerned. For example, in Vancouver there has been a question as to whether the British Columbia Electric Railway Company Limited should reduce its transit fares by reason of receiving this income tax benefit. Judging from the press reports no one is clear as to whether or not that will be the effect. It would be helpful if the minister could give some explanation of the way in which this amendment will benefit the general public.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is a little difficult to do that except in general terms, as my hon. friend will appreciate. The net effect of this section will be that the effective rate of income tax on the earnings of certain corporations from certain types of activity-that is, the generation, distribution and sale for delivery in Canada of electrical energy, gas and steam-will be taxed at that rate, but only the earnings from that portion of its activities. If a company were carrying on varied activities-running a railway, running a street railway line, running a mine and doing a lot of other things-it is only the earnings from these particular activities which will be subject to the reduced rate of tax. The reduction is for the reasons I gave in my budget speech, which I do not suppose I need repeat here. The effect would be different with respect to different companies. Broadly speaking it parallels the provision which the committee will recall was contained in our general offer to the provinces in connection with the tax rental agreements, namely that we remit to the provinces

one-half of our tax revenues from these sources. That was accepted as being the test. It was the same group of earnings that we considered should be subject to this special rate. The rate can be down to 43 per cent; I am now speaking over-all.
The money which was turned over to the provinces under the previous scheme would, in effect, be the same as if they had taxed the companies. ,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; not quite that. We turn over half of our income. In other words, if we get $2 million, let us say for the sake of an example, from the electric earnings of the British Columbia Electric Company-I just use that as an example; I do not say that we get that amount-we would just turn over $1 million to the province of British Columbia.
But in this particular case the British Columbia Electric Company will have to pay a smaller amount of taxes. In the earlier case it did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course. The British Columbia Electric Company-taking that company as an example-would pay a 43 per cent rate on its sales to the public of electricity, gas or steam. It is quite obvious that since we were turning over half of whatever we got from that company, the amount which would be turned over to the province of British Columbia would be somewhat reduced.
I am not worrying about the amount that would be turned over to the province of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know that.
What worries me is whether the people who have to pay for this light and gas will be entitled to any reduction in their rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not express any opinion on that matter until I saw what the amount of the tax saving, if any, amounted to. I suppose it would be a matter to be taken into account by the public utilities board of British Columbia which fixes the rates of these companies. That was one of the reasons which prompted this rather modest and temporary-I hope and believe-tax concession. It was thought that it might prevent some further applications for rate increases in this type of concern.

I am glad the minister has made this point clear because from his statement in his budget speech what it was taken to mean, or what I believe the company is arguing, is that this was for the purpose of enabling the company to raise money more
Income Tax Act
readily than it had been doing, and that there was nothing to be passed on to the general public.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter for the company to fight out, of course, with any rateregulating body. The essential thing is that any privately-owned public utility must be in a position to raise a portion of the capital it needs for expansion, as equity capital; and it can only do so if it is able to show a reasonably good earnings record. Otherwise it cannot. I think it is generally recognized that it is unsound to have a capital structure-in the case of public utilities or in that of any other company-which is top heavy so far as borrowed capital is concerned. The question as to whether the earnings on equity capital are so great that they justify rate reductions or are so low that they justify rate increases is a matter for the regulating bodies; for the provincial rate-regulating body if it is a utility under provincial jurisdiction, or for the board of transport commissioners if it happens to be a utility that is subject to the jurisdiction of that board.
But this reduction will in effect result in greater income to these companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It should result in greater net income. How much more I am not in a position to say.
It will result in greater net income; and as far as the minister is concerned, there is in the section nothing which would prevent the companies from giving lower rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter that is entirely within the control of the companies and the rate-regulating bodies. It is not in my control.
This clause will have a tendency to bring more nearly into line the activities of privately-owned utility corporations and those of publicly-owned corporations, I presume.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is bound to have that tendency.
It is just one step. It is a small step, but nevertheless it helps.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is true of any corporation, is it not?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Is the Prime Minister going to make a statement in addition to what has already been placed before the house?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: I do not intend to make a statement at this time. I shall be glad to answer any questions in the committee stage that I am in a position to answer. I think the reception this proposal received from the house at the resolution stage shows that there is nothing controversial about it and that all members of the house are happy that at least this initial step is being taken at this time, and are hopeful that further steps may not be too long delayed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:

National Library

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: At the present time the act will be under the administration of the Secretary of State. At some later stage another minister may be put in charge of this and other like activities of the Canadian government, but for the initial stages it is intended to have this measure, like the archives, under the administration of the Secretary of State.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-National librarian.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: My question really deals with sections 4 and 5. I should like to ask whether it is proposed to appoint a national librarian immediately and also an assistant national librarian.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: It is intended to appoint immediately as national librarian Dr. Lamb, who is now in charge of the archives, and to have him organize the preliminary steps. An assistant librarian would not necessarily be appointed immediately. That would be done as and when Dr. Lamb recommends that sufficient advance has been made to require the services of an assistant librarian.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Will Dr. Lamb be able to retain his present position as archivist?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Yes. I explained at the resolution stage that, although the Massey commission recommended that ultimately there be separate heads for the archives and the national library, they also recommended that initially the archivist should have charge of the organizational stages of the national library.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT

Should there not be some definition of their positions?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:

national library it was felt that these two officials should be part of the advisory council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: I agree with the proposition that they should be members of the council. The only question that arises in my mind is as to whether any uncertainty could occur at any time with respect to what these positions actually were. I recognize that it relates to positions that we understand at the present time. subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT

I recognize that it is not possible in advance to place too exact an interpretation upon provisions that are adopted at this time, but I do recall the point that was made by one of the hon. members when this was in the resolution stage. I would hope this would be the appropriate time to point out that it would be highly desirable that there should be no attempt to exclude from the library books dealing with subjects that might not ordinarily be regarded as subjects that we would wish to have dealt with too generally throughout the country. I am referring, for instance, to the possibility of the books published with relation to systems of government with which we very strongly disagree, or matters of that kind, being excluded. Not only should they not be excluded, but we should do our best to obtain them because we should make available here as complete documentary records of other systems of government and other matters of that kind as we possibly can. I merely make this observation now because I realize that this is going to provide the preliminary setting for the establishment of a national library.
May I for the last time in. relation to this point indicate that there may be some possibility at a later stage of defining the positions with greater accuracy, because I am sure the hon. member for Greenwood uses the library as much as any member in the house; and when I find he does not know which officials are described under the terms employed here, then it does suggest to me the desirability of defining these official positions.

The officials who are described in this legislation as the parliamentary librarian and the general librarian have been performing a very great and very efficient service on behalf of hon. members, and for that reason on behalf of the people of Canada. The remarks made by the leader of the opposition will be a part of the record, and I am sure that both the law officers and Dr. Lamb will take those remarks into account. Doubtless at some early date further legislation will be required as the work of organizing the national library proceeds. At that time I am sure the law officers will take into account the remarks made by the leader of the opposition with respect to having the librarians of parliament associated in some permanent way with the work of the national library.
I am sure also that Dr. Lamb will recognize the views expressed in this house as to the desirability of having available, for perhaps only limited use but having available there, books that it might not be desirable to circulate widely to the public, but which should be available for those who are specially interested in problems on which those books will have a bearing. I am sure it will be the desire of those responsible for the content of the library to have it a reliable reference library where students will find the books that it may be difficult for them to secure elsewhere.

speechtext:
I should like to deal for a moment with paragraph (e) of section 10. I think the wording is unfortunate, but there may be some explanation for it. We are told that the national librarian may:
Generally supervise and direct the work of the national library in such a manner that the facilities of the library may be made available to the government and people of Canada-
Perhaps they might also be made available to the opposition. Perhaps it would be advisable to put in the word "parliament" instead of "government".

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: I think here the word "government" is not used to describe the executive; it is used to describe the whole machinery of government which comprises His Excellency the Governor General and the two houses of parliament. That is the official status of the houses of parliament, the members supporting the executive and the members opposing the executive. I am sure it was certainly not intended to make it available exclusively to those who happen to constitute, for the time being, the advisers to the representative of the sovereign. The wording is used to describe in a rather wider sense the whole social organization for the government of the country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I accept the Prime Minister's explanation, but I must say that I have said some very nasty things about His Excellency if we accept this connotation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Is there any reason for including the words, "to the government and the people of Canada"?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT

I do not think there is, but it was to follow out the idea that there would have to be transferred almost at once from various government departments books which are now in those separate departments. They are all being catalogued so they may become available to the general public through this catalogue. I think that was the reason the expression was used here.
It is not intended to duplicate, for instance, the collection of scientific books that are in the national research council; but they will form a part of the union catalogue, and when inquiry is made the national librarian will be able to secure them from wherever they are and make them available to those who have reason to consult them. It was not intended to imply that the members of the government, any more than the members of the opposition, were not a part of the people of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Perhaps it is intended to imply they need the books more.

On section 11 -Deposit of books with librarian.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Is this section patterned on the practice elsewhere? As I read it, it winds up with a penalty of a fine on summary conviction, which seems a little severe. I understand the requirement of getting books into the library, but I just wanted to ask whether the section in its present form is usual or whether there is a precedent for it. I presume it is common sense to get a copy of every book sent in, and perhaps if it is you need to wind up the section with a penalty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I am informed that this provision is usually in all the statutes creating national libraries. The requirements here are not nearly as onerous as those which exist under the corresponding statute in the United Kingdom, where there is a requirement that books be supplied to the national library, to the university of Oxford, to the university of Cambridge, and I think there is one other university which has the right by statute to have books supplied.
This section is a repetition, perhaps in more precise form, of what is already in the Copyright Act. Section 11 of chapter 8 of the statutes of 1931 provides:
The publisher of every book published in Canada, within three months after the publication thereof, shall deliver or cause to be delivered, at his own expense, to the librarian of parliament, who shall give a written receipt therefor, two copies of the

first edition and two copies of each subsequent edition if such subsequent edition contains additions or alterations either in the letter press or in the maps, prints or other engravings thereto belonging.
When there is no sanction expressly provided, there is a general provision in the Criminal Code that is much more severe than the one provided here. Anyone who wilfully violates a statutory requirement for which violation no special penalty is provided is liable to prosecution-I do not know the number of the section, but under a section with which the hon. member is as familiar as I am-under a section which provides much more severe penalties than those provided here. I believe the reason for including this section was to have the act self-contained, and not have to rely on this provision of the Criminal Code in case there was a violation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
My fear
was really that the person who would actually have to provide the money would not be the wealthy publisher but the poor author. I suppose the answer is that these expensive books that are referred to here will probably be the exceptional case, and the two copies provided will not be impossible even for a poor author writing his first book.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: This section apparently covers books published in Canada, but what policy is adopted to acquire books from the United Kingdom and the United States from outstanding authors and publishers?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: If the book is published in Canada-it does not necessarily have to be printed in Canada-or if it is distributed in Canada by a Canadian publisher, he would be required to supply these copies unless exemption was provided. During the resolution stage I explained that it was intended to require the deposit of books by Canadian authors, whether printed in Canada or elsewhere, and also of books which dealt mainly with matters of Canadian concern, so the Canadian national library might become the most complete collection of books published by Canadians or books dealing with matters of special concern to Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I do not want to appear to be splitting hairs about the wording of this act, but I am somewhat concerned about the provision requiring two copies of every book that is published. In looking at the definition of the word "book", it seems to me this would cover every conceivable kind of thing that is printed in this country which could be regarded as reading material. In the definitive section of the act the word "book" is described as including library matter of every kind, nature and description. I should

think that even the smallest periodical publication, whether it be a daily, weekly or monthly, would be library matter of some kind. Certainly libraries do include that material, but I do not know whether this section would be wide enough to oblige every publisher of some of these scandal sheets, tipster sheets or publications of that kind, which are all too numerous, or even much more serious publications of a very simple nature to be filed in this way.
I should think this would present a very serious problem for the librarians and their staff if it should be that wide. I think we should carefully consider whether or not that is the effect of the combined wording of section 11 and the definition in section 2. It gets back to the inquiry that was previously directed to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as to whether this follows the general pattern of similar statutes in other jurisdictions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I was informed by Dr. Lamb that it was a less stringent requirement than those in the United Kingdom or in France. There is a provision that the minister may make regulations respecting the quality of the copies required to be delivered to the national library of any book the copies of which are not of uniform quality; prescribing generally the classes or kinds of books in respect of which one copy is required to be delivered to the national librarian; and prescribing the classes or kinds of books in respect of which no copies are required to be delivered. That is within our regulations that will be made under statutory authority, which will require to be published under the Regulations Act.
It may be that experience will show that there should be something more specific in the statutory provision. I compared it with the requirement in chapter 32 of the revised statutes with respect to the Copyright Act and this definition did not appear to me to include	as	much	as	was	included	in	thedefinition in the Copyright Act. definition of "book" in the Copyright Act.
It was pointed out to me that we certainly did not want to provide housing space for copies of everything that was published or issued in Canada in writing or picture form. which no copies are required to be delivered to the national librarian.

I should
like to add a word, Mr. Chairman. I was impressed by the point made by the leader of the opposition. I am just wondering whether there might be something invidious in describing the classes of books of which no copies are required and whether it might not have been better to do it the other way and describe the classes of books of which copies are required. I raise that point for consideration. It seems to me that if a list is produced some time, describing the kinds of books of which no copies are required, that might be open to a certain invidious interpretation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I do not intend to labour the point following what has just been said, but I would point out this situation. We are dealing with an act which lays the foundation for the delivery to the national iibrary of publications in Canada which are described as books. I would be inclined to think that with the passing of this act anyone who was publishing even the smallest kind of periodical of any kind and was aware of this requirement-and who, quite apart from the possible fine of $25, did not want the nuisance involved in a thing of that kind-would make inquiries as to whether, in the absence of any specific regulation against his type of publication, he might not be called upon to deliver it.
I must confess that if the Prime Minister were consulted as a lawyer he would likely say: Unless there is some exemption, you are required to deliver it, having regard to the definition of "book" in section 2. If that is the answer the Prime Minister or any other lawyer would give, we are immediately confronted with the fact that until such time as the exemptions have been adopted, defining books that are not to be delivered, the moment this act goes into effect everyone who publishes anything that could come within the wide definition in section 2 would immediately be called upon to deliver it to the librarian unless he wanted to take the chance of getting into some difficulty at some later date.
I am not going to labour that point unduly. I recognize the fact that we are still in the preliminary stages; but it seems to me that this is a good time to avoid any unnecessary piling up of useless material in the hands of the librarian here in Ottawa.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I would have to tell him that his obligation was no greater than it had been at any time since the adoption of the Copyright Act of 1931, because that was

speakerposition: topic

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The parties to the North Atlantic treaty, signed at Washington on 4th April 1949,
Being satisfied that the creation of the European defence community set up under the treaty signed at Paris on	will
strengthen the North Atlantic community and the integrated defence of the North Atlantic area, and promote the closer association of the countries of western Europe, and
Considering that the parties to the treaty setting up the European defence community have signed a protocol, which will enter into force at the same time as the present protocol, giving to the parties to the North Atlantic treaty guarantees equivalent to the guarantees contained in article 5 of the North Atlantic treaty,
Agree as follows:
Article I
An armed attack
(i)	on the territory of any of the members of the European defence community in Europe or in the area described in article 6 (i) of the North Atlantic treaty, or
(ii)	on the forces, vessels or aircraft of the European defence community when in the area described in article 6 (ii) of the said treaty,
shall be considered an attack against all the parties to the North Atlantic treaty, within the meaning of article 5 of the said treaty, and article 5 shall apply accordingly.
The expression 'member of the European defence community' in paragraph (i) of this article means any of the following states which is a member of the community, namely, Belgium, France, the German Federal Republic, Italy, Luxembourg, and The Netherlands.
Article II
The present protocol shall enter into force as soon as each of the parties has notified the government of the United States of America of its acceptance and the council of the European defence community has notified the North Atlantic council of the entry into force of the treaty setting up the European defence community. The government of the United States of America shall inform all the parties to the North Atlantic treaty of the date of the receipt of each such notification and of the date of the entry into force of the present protocol.
Article III
The present protocol shall remain in force for so long as the North Atlantic treaty and the treaty setting up the European defence community remain in force and the parties to the latter treaty continue to give, in respect of themselves and the European defence forces, guarantees to the parties to the North Atlantic treaty equivalent to the guarantees contained in the present protocol.
Article IY
The present protocol, of which the English and French texts are equally authentic, shall be deposited in the archives of the government of the United States of America. Duly certified copies thereof shall be transmitted by that government to the governments of all the parties to the North Atlantic treaty and of all the parties to the treaty setting up the European defence community.
In witness whereof, the undersigned plenipotentiaries have signed the present protocol.
